paragraphs.heading: Seven bright stars
paragraphs.text: The Big Dipper, known as the Plough in the UK and Ireland, is an asterism made of seven bright stars that belong to Ursa Major. Six shine at second magnitude, and one, Megrez, is of third magnitude. Four stars make up a bowl or body, and the other three make a handle or head. Many cultures recognize it as a group of its own.

paragraphs.heading: A pointer to the North Star
paragraphs.text: The two front stars of the pattern, Merak and Dubhe, are sometimes called the Pointers. Extend an imaginary line through them and it leads to Polaris, the North Star, today's northern pole star, which also marks the end of the Little Dipper's handle. That is why the Big Dipper is useful in celestial navigation.

paragraphs.heading: A bear or a wagon
paragraphs.text: Ursa Major, Latin for Greater Bear, has been imagined in many shapes: a bear, a plough, a wagon, even a ladle. The bear idea is Indo-European, found in Greece and in Vedic India, while the wagon, or wain, idea comes from Mesopotamia. Book XVIII of Homer's Iliad calls it the Bear that people also call the Wain. Classical Greek stories said the Bear was the nymph Callisto, whom Zeus's jealous wife Hera changed into a she-bear. In Latin the seven stars were the Seven Oxen.

paragraphs.heading: Names across Europe
paragraphs.text: In Britain and Ireland the pattern is the Plough, and the Starry Plough has served as a political symbol for Irish Republican and left-wing movements. Former names include the Great Wain, Arthur's Wain and Butcher's Cleaver. A folk story ties the name Charles's Wain to Charlemagne, but the name is shared across the Germanic languages and first meant the men's wagon, set against the women's wagon, which is the Little Dipper. Germans usually call it the Great Wagon, and Dutch speakers popularly call it the Saucepan.

paragraphs.heading: A funeral and a bow
paragraphs.text: An Arabic name for the pattern, Banāt Naʿsh, means the daughters of the bier, a bier being a funeral litter. In this picture the four stars of the bowl are the bier and the three handle stars are mourners walking behind it. In the Sámi languages of Northern Europe, the stars are seen as the bow of the great hunter Fávdna.

paragraphs.heading: The Northern Dipper
paragraphs.text: In Chinese astronomy the Big Dipper is called Beidou, which literally means Northern Dipper. Star records from the Warring States period, around 475 to 221 BCE, describe it as seven stars shaped like a dipper or a chariot. These Chinese records were later translated into other East Asian cultures. Its best-known names there are the Northern Dipper and the Seven Stars of the Northern Dipper.
